prime.problem: Decoding writes one token per full read of the weights, and the chip mostly waits on memory. A single pass could check several tokens for about the same memory cost, if only something could propose them.
prime.fits: Fifth mechanism card. The earlier cards changed bandwidth or bytes per token; this one changes the third factor, tokens produced per read of the weights. It's the trick behind many fast hosts.
prime.goal: Estimate the speed-up for a given acceptance rate and draft cost, and say when speculative decoding helps and when it hurts.

attend: Why does checking 5 guessed tokens cost about the same as writing 1 token?
Why is the output identical to what the big model would have written alone?
What happens to the speed-up when the draft guesses badly?
Why does the gain shrink from up to 6.5× at one request to 1.38× at 64 requests at once?
Why doesn't it improve time to first token?

must: Decode is memory-bound → one weight read can score several positions for about the same cost → a cheap draft proposes k tokens and the big model verifies them in one pass → several tokens per slow pass
The big model keeps every guess it agrees with and replaces the first wrong one → the output is what the big model would have written → speed goes up with no quality change
Speed-up depends on acceptance → tokens per pass = (1 − α<sup>k+1</sup>) ÷ (1 − α) against draft cost → high α on predictable text (code) wins, low α can be slower than plain decoding
elevated: Busy servers already fill each weight read with many users' tokens → less spare capacity to verify guesses → the gain shrinks with load (EAGLE-3: 1.38× at 64 concurrent)
reference: the made-up 6.5 ms draft cost in the example

compress.prompt: From memory, explain speculative decoding in 3–4 sentences to someone who knows decode is memory-bound. Then compute the average speed-up for α = 0.8, k = 4 and a draft costing 0.1 of a big pass.
checklist: a small draft guesses k tokens; the big model checks them in one pass
accept matching guesses, fix the first mismatch: output unchanged
it works because the check costs about one memory read, like writing one token
(1 − 0.8<sup>5</sup>) ÷ 0.2 = 3.36 tokens per pass; 1.4 pass-units of time; ≈ 2.4×
helps writing only, and less on busy servers

retrieve.q: Explain why speculative decoding doesn't change the output, while switching to the small model would.
answer: the big model verifies every token and replaces any it disagrees with
only tokens the big model would have produced are kept
the small model alone would keep its own, lower-quality choices

retrieve.q: Walk through the two big-model passes in the for i in range(1, 101): example: what's guessed, what's accepted, and how many tokens each pass yields.
answer: pass 1: for · i · in · range all accepted, plus ( added free: 5 tokens
pass 2: 1 and , accepted, 100 rejected and replaced with 101: 3 tokens
8 tokens in 2 passes: 182 ms vs 519 ms, ≈ 2.9×

retrieve.q: You're generating creative fiction with a high temperature on a busy shared server. Is speculative decoding worth enabling? Give two reasons.
answer: creative, high-temperature text is hard to guess, so acceptance is low
a busy server has little spare capacity to verify guesses
you pay the draft and may end up slower than plain decoding

compare.q: Both raise tokens/s on the same hardware. Which factor of "bandwidth ÷ bytes × tokens per pass" does each change, and which one changes the output?
answer: quantization cuts bytes per token; speculative decoding raises tokens per pass
quantization changes the weights, so outputs can shift and quality can drop
speculative decoding leaves the output exactly as the big model would write it

compare.q: This card uses a greedy example. How does speculative sampling keep the output distribution exact when tokens are sampled, not picked greedily?
answer: accept a draft token with probability min(1, p<sub>target</sub> ÷ p<sub>draft</sub>)
on rejection, sample from the normalised leftover (p<sub>target</sub> − p<sub>draft</sub>)<sup>+</sup>
so the output distribution matches the target model exactly

predict.q: Keep k = 4 and draft cost 0.1, but drop acceptance to α = 0.6 (less predictable text). Predict the speed-up before computing, and whether it's still worth it.
predict.answer: Tokens per pass = (1 − 0.6<sup>5</sup>) ÷ 0.4 ≈ 2.31; time per pass is still 1.4 units; speed-up ≈ 1.65×. Still a win, but much smaller than 2.4×. As α falls further the ratio approaches 1 ÷ 1.4, a slowdown.

apply.task: By hand or in a few lines of Python, tabulate the speed-up for α = 0.5, 0.7, 0.9 and k = 2, 4, 8 with draft cost 0.1 per guess. Find the break-even α for k = 4 (speed-up = 1), and say which k you'd pick for code and which for chat.
apply.done: Your table has 9 cells computed with (1 − α<sup>k+1</sup>) ÷ (1 − α) ÷ (0.1k + 1), your α = 0.8, k = 4 check gives ≈ 2.4, and you've found a break-even α for k = 4.
apply.hint: At break-even, tokens per pass = 1.4 for k = 4. Try α around 0.3.
